opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. My background is in more general machine learning, and coming into protein modeling, the first thing you notice is how much of the field has historically been built on carefully hand-engineered components: specialized geometric modules, domain-specific featurization, and a lot of baked-in priors about how proteins should look. Those were incredibly important for getting us to where we are. AlphaFold2 was a landmark partly because of how cleverly it encoded structural intuition into the architecture.

But the lesson from the rest of machine learning, the "bitter lesson" if you want to call it that, is that over time the general methods that scale with data and compute tend to win. So at Chai, a big part of how we approach things is asking: which of these inductive biases are actually necessary, and which ones are crutches we can remove if we have the right training setup and enough signal?

In practice that means a few things. First, we try to use architectures that look a lot like what works elsewhere: transformers, diffusion-style generative modeling, and so on, rather than inventing a bespoke module for every sub-problem. Second, we think hard about representation. Proteins, small molecules, nucleic acids, and post-translational modifications can all be treated in a more unified way, at the level of tokens and atoms, so one model can reason about a whole complex instead of having a separate pipeline for each molecule type. Third, we lean on things like language-model embeddings and evolutionary information as inputs, and we try to make the model robust when some of that information is missing. Not every target has a deep multiple sequence alignment, especially in drug discovery settings.

That said, I don't think it's purely a "throw a transformer at it" story. Biology is data-limited in ways that text and images aren't. You might have a couple hundred thousand experimental structures in the PDB, and that's tiny compared with internet-scale data. So some of the craft is figuring out where a little bit of structure in the model, or a smart training objective, buys you a lot of sample efficiency. There's also the evaluation question. In protein modeling it's really easy to fool yourself with data leakage between train and test sets, so we put a lot of care into benchmarking on things that reflect how these models get used in the real world.

So the short version: we start from general ML principles, we're skeptical of complexity that doesn't earn its keep, and then we're pragmatic about the places where biology really does demand something special.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that the biggest lesson from the last few years of machine learning, in language and in vision, is that general-purpose architectures trained at scale on the right data tend to beat clever, hand-crafted domain-specific systems. And structural biology was, for a really long time, the opposite of that. It was a field built on physics-based force fields, hand-tuned energy functions, and a lot of expert intuition baked into the pipeline.

What AlphaFold2 showed is that you don't necessarily need all of that. You can learn a lot of it from data. But even AlphaFold2 had a ton of domain-specific machinery in it. Invariant point attention, the triangle updates, a very bespoke structure module. And a lot of the thinking at Chai is, how much of that is actually necessary, and how much of it is scaffolding we can strip away as we get more data and more compute?

So when we were building Chai-1, the philosophy was really to lean on things we know work generally. Diffusion as the generative process over coordinates, because it's a clean, well-understood framework and it lets you treat proteins, small molecules, nucleic acids, all as one unified problem instead of building a separate model for each. Transformer-style attention over tokens, where a token might be a residue or an atom. And then being very deliberate about where you add inductive bias, rather than adding it everywhere by default.

The honest answer, though, is that biology still fights you a little. The data is small compared to text. The PDB is a couple hundred thousand structures, and they're heavily biased toward what crystallographers could get to crystallize. So you can't just throw a vanilla model at it and walk away. You spend a lot of time on data curation, on how you handle homology and leakage in your splits, on what you condition on, like MSAs or templates or experimental restraints. That's where a lot of the real engineering lives.

And then the other piece is that the end users aren't ML researchers, they're chemists and biologists. So "general" also has to mean the model does something useful on their actual problems, which are usually very far from the training distribution. A novel binder, a target that has no close homologs. That's the part I find most interesting, honestly. Making the models general enough that they keep working when the data runs out.

r003.rationale: It does not mention ESM or attribute transformer success to abundant protein sequence data.

r004.rationale: It says structural biology data is small compared with text, describes the limited and biased set of PDB structures, and explains why a vanilla model cannot simply be applied.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is figuring out which parts of the problem benefit from general machine-learning methods and which parts really need biological or physical structure built in. You can think of a protein as a sequence, but what you ultimately care about is a three-dimensional object and how it interacts with other molecules. So the representation and the training objective matter a lot.

The approach I’d take is to start with methods that scale well, then ask where they’re missing something essential about the problem. You want the model to learn as much as possible from data, while giving it the right structure to reason about geometry and interactions. And you have to evaluate whether it captures the biology you care about, rather than just getting better at a convenient prediction task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to ask which parts of the problem really require protein-specific assumptions and which parts you can let the model learn. Proteins have a lot of structure, so you want to represent the geometry correctly and respect the symmetries of the problem. But you don’t necessarily want to hand-engineer every interaction you think matters.

At Chai, the way I think about it is to bring those general machine-learning ideas—learning rich representations, training on diverse data, and scaling—to a problem where the output is a physical structure. The interesting challenge is making that work across interacting molecules, rather than treating each protein as an isolated object.

And ultimately, a plausible-looking structure isn’t the whole goal. You want predictions that help someone make a better experimental decision. That’s where the modeling choices have to prove useful.
